draft.title: Research methods
card: a researcher asks one person questions in depth. It suits personal experiences and reasons, and it can follow up answers.
a set of written questions given to many people. It suits finding how common an opinion or behaviour is across a large group.
a small group discusses a topic together. It shows how views are shared, challenged or changed in a group.
the researcher watches behaviour without joining in. In participant observation the researcher takes part in the group while studying it.
draft.remember: Choose the method that fits the question: depth from a few people, patterns from many, or what people actually do.

a.q: A researcher wants to know how common late-night social media use is among students at a large school. Which method suits this best?
opts: A questionnaire given to many students
A focus group of five students
a.why: A questionnaire reaches many people with the same questions, so it shows how common a behaviour is. An interview gives depth, but from one person it cannot show how common the behaviour is across a large school.
a.clue: The question asks how common something is across many people.

b.q: Priya wants to study how a local football club's members behave and what the club's unwritten rules are. She joins the club as a player and records what she sees. Which method is she using?
b.why: Priya takes part in the group while studying it, so this is participant observation. It is not plain observation, because in that method the researcher watches without joining in.
b.clue: Does Priya watch from outside or take part in the group?

a.best: A questionnaire given to many students

problems.detail: The clue says the question is about 'many people', and only the right option says 'many students'. A student can match the words without knowing what a questionnaire suits.

The remember line sorts the methods into three neat types (depth from a few, patterns from many, what people do), which the card does not do. Focus groups, which show how views change in a group, do not fit any of the three.
The point lists content analysis, case studies and statistical analysis as research methods, but the card leaves all three out. Students only meet half the methods the point is meant to teach.

proposal.title: Research methods
card: An interview asks one person questions in depth, so it suits personal experiences and reasons. A questionnaire gives the same written questions to many people, so it suits finding how common a view or behaviour is.

A focus group is a small group discussing a topic, which shows how views are shared, challenged or changed. In observation the researcher watches without joining in, and in participant observation they take part in the group.
Content analysis studies media or documents, such as ads, films or news stories, by counting or interpreting what they contain. A case study looks closely at one person, group, place or event.
Statistical analysis uses numbers, such as census figures, to find trends and compare groups over time.
proposal.remember: Start with the research question, then choose the method whose strengths fit it.

a.q: A researcher wants to find out how often women are shown as leaders in Australian TV ads. Which method suits this best?
a.why: The evidence sits in the ads themselves, and content analysis counts or interprets what media contain. An interview gives depth about what one person thinks, but it cannot measure what the ads actually show.
a.clue: Is the evidence found in people or in the ads?

b.clue: Does Priya watch from outside or take part in the group?
